MorphoHand · SR2 hand, real_v1 screwdriver · servo plant, hand-object control and RL contact cost · 6 October 2026 · built 2026-10-07 10:09

Servo plant refit, hand-object control of the three-finger turn, and the cost of sphere-pad fingertips in RL training

The deployed open-loop three-finger turn holds the tool on 40 of 40 placements and turns it 27–57° in MuJoCo once the scene carries the servo response the bench readbacks show (0.02 s instead of 1 s), friction near 1 and the tool resting on its post. The relative contact-velocity controller of Wang, Oh and Pollard, keeping all three contacts and regulating pad force, holds 40 of 40 placements but stops at 6–42°, because the deployed grips leave the pips no extension; without its stop rule it drops the tool on 6 of 8 hands. Sphere pads at 1 mm cost 12 % of RL env throughput at 2,048 envs, because physics is a small part of an env step; from one held RL state the pads cost 2.2–2.4 µs of physics per world-step in MuJoCo-Warp, Newton’s hydroelastic contact on the plain fingertip shape 4.3 µs, point contact 0.6–1.4 µs. SolverMuJoCo realises Newton’s hydroelastic stiffness times the tip–tool effective mass; with divided by that mass the deployed plans hold the tool on 33 of 40 placements in Newton (10 uncorrected) and turn it within 5° of MuJoCo on 5 of 8 hands. Against Drake, the 1 mm pads agree to the same degree in CPU MuJoCo, MuJoCo-Warp and Newton (twist onset torque 0.94–0.94 of Drake’s; plan turn within 3° of Drake on 23 / 23 / 22 of 24 placements). Trained from scratch for 20 M steps on the working plant, the D6 reorientation ends at cos 0.64–0.69 with the TPU block as one mesh and 0.43–0.44 with 1 mm pads, holding the tool in 60–64 of 64 rollouts; no run reaches cos 0.9, and the pad envs need 640 contacts and 3,072 constraint rows per world. The 2026-09-02 servo-gain fit closed the fingers on air; the bench readbacks fix the finger time constant and favour but do not identify the gain.

Terms and metrics

tool turn
rotation of the tool’s axis from its pose at the end of the grip, in the vertical plane through the axis, in degrees; positive toward vertical, 90° = standing on end. The open-loop replays measure it from the cosine of the axis with vertical, which equals the same angle for a tool starting flat.
held
at the end of the rollout the tool is within 20 mm of its height at the end of the grip and at least two fingers touch it.
held peak
the largest tool turn reached while the tool was held in that sense (any time in the rollout).
joint readback error
mean over the nine finger joints and over the bench’s three servo readbacks of one run (before the turn, during it, at the settled hold) of |simulated − bench achieved angle|, in degrees; the replay applies the run’s own logged command frames at their logged times.
servo position gain of the simulated finger actuator, N m/rad: joint torque for command and angle , clipped at the torque limit.
time constant
finger joint damping divided by , in seconds: the time a free finger joint takes to cover 63 % of a step command (actuator velocity gain 0).
Coulomb friction coefficient of the fingertip pads on the tool.
pads
the printed TPU block (17 × 14.8 × 22 mm, 2.7 mm fillets on the front and end edges) covered with 0.75 mm spheres at 1 mm spacing (1,059 per tip; 290 at 2 mm); stiffness per sphere area with = 10 MPa, = 8.5 mm, reached at load through solimp.
HOM controller
the relative contact-velocity controller of Wang, Oh and Pollard (arXiv 2609.25619): per fingertip, a contact frame from the closest points of tip and tool, joint rates from bounded least squares on reference relative velocities (their Eq. 2). Defined in Section 3.
governor
the HOM controller’s stop rule: when a pad’s normal force falls below 30 % of its target or the tool lags the reference by more than 6°, the reference stops and the angle reached is held.
inverse weight
MuJoCo’s body_invweight0[b, 0]: the translational inverse inertia of body at the model’s reference pose, in 1/kg, computed at compile time from the joint-space mass matrix; for a free body of mass , and for a fingertip the inverse of the inertia the whole finger chain and its servo armature present at the tip.
effective mass
of a contact between bodies 1 and 2: , in kg. MuJoCo’s solref is a spring on the constraint acceleration, so a contact realises its solref stiffness times as a force stiffness.
hydroelastic stiffness of a Newton shape, in N/m³: pressure per unit penetration depth, for an elastic layer of modulus and thickness .
solimp impedance of a sphere pad (constant over penetration), set so that each pad contact is a spring of stiffness ; see Eq. (4).
sink
steady penetration of each pad into the tool in the contact bed’s static pinch, in mm, after 1 s at the set normal force with gravity off; Drake hydroelastic gives 0.153, 0.213 and 0.365 mm at 0.5, 1 and 3 N.
onset torque
contact bed, twist task: a torque about the pinch axis ramps up on the pinched tool; the onset torque is the last value at which the spin speed still follows the creep law , in mN m. Drake hydroelastic gives 0.84, 1.97 and 7.65 mN m at 0.5, 1 and 3 N.
creep rate
the slope of the creep law below the onset torque, in °/s per mN m; rigid Coulomb friction gives 0.
largest swing
contact bed, brake task: the pinch on the tool, whose centre of mass sits 15 mm off the pinch line, is held at 6 N for 0.5 s and lowered geometrically to 0.2 N over 4 s; the largest swing is the largest angle of the tool axis below horizontal over the run, in degrees (90° = hanging). Drake hydroelastic gives 87.3°.
grip force
sum of the three fingertips’ normal forces on the tool at the end of the hold of an open-loop plan replay, in N.
within 3°
a plan replay whose tool turn at the end is within 3° of Drake’s on the same hand and placement, with the tool held in both.
env steps/s
policy steps per second summed over all parallel environments of the RL training env; one env step is 10 physics steps of 2 ms plus observations, rewards and terminations.
physics µs per world-step
wall time of one batched physics step divided by the number of worlds.

Bench post and servo plant

The post under the tool

Scene.set_object_platform(height) now puts the post’s top at the tool’s lowest point, computed from the compiled geometry (height − 12.5 mm for the flat 25 mm tool), and keeps height as the tool’s centre, which the exported plans’ grip poses refer to. Stored scenes are repaired on load by seated_scene(path), which writes <stem>__seated.xml beside the original. plant_drop_gate.py, real_v1_bench_plants.py, real_v1_turn_mechanism.py, plant_ranking_test.py, real_v1_plan_angle_sweep.py, real_v1_tip_gait.py and calibrate_plant_kp.py load scenes through it. In the D7 scene the post top moved from 100.0 to 87.5 mm and the tool’s initial penetration of the post from 12.5 mm to 0.

The 2026-09-02 gain fit never loaded a finger

calibrate_plant_kp.py reset each candidate scene from its keyframe 0, which puts the palm at 10 mm; the plan’s replay state puts it at 103.5 mm, above the tool on its 100 mm post. The fingers closed on air while the palm rested against the tool and the post, so the +11.09° middle-yaw deficit that matched the bench’s +11.68° at  = 0.5 came from the fingers’ own response, with no load from the tool (time constant 1.04 s at  = 0.5 with the template’s joint damping 0.5, read 2 s after the last command). The script now starts from the plan’s replay state; its fit is superseded by the replays below.

Replaying the bench’s own runs

The archive holds 177 complete reorientation runs of the eight deployed hands with servo readbacks and AprilTag tracking (D1 43, D2 11, D3 19, D4 23, D5 20, D6 21, D7 16, D8 24). bench_replay_calibration.py rebuilds each run on its hand’s bench scene (palm welded at the plan’s pose, tool resting on the repaired post, TPU pads, 1 ms step, elliptic cone, impratio 100), holds the plan’s grip for 0.8 s, applies the run’s logged command frames at their logged times and compares the nine joint angles at the run’s three servo readbacks. The plant is set on the compiled model: , joint damping (actuator velocity gain 0), torque limit, joint friction. A coarse grid of 252 servo settings at and 2.4 on the median-turn run of each hand and a finer grid of 144 plants on three runs per hand preceded the full replay in Table 1.

The readbacks fix two things. The finger time constant is short: at or below 0.2 s gives 2.53–2.63° and 0.6 s gives 3.60°, which rules out the 1 s fingers every calibrated-plant result since 2026-09-16 ran on. Friction near 1 fits better than the scenes’ 2.4 by about 1°. The servo gain is not identified: across  = 0.25–30 the best error stays within 2.53–2.75°, because a finger pressing on the tool stops at the tool, and its deficit is set by the grip geometry, whatever the stiffness behind it. The torque limit is not identified either. The fit’s cost also included the tool’s tracked tilt, and with it the best plants had = 2–10 and between 0.8 and 1.3; bench task outcomes depend on how the tool was placed and on contacts the scene does not model, so that part of the fit is not used here.

The rest of this page runs the working plant: = 4 N m/rad, 0.02 s (joint damping 0.08), torque limit 1 N m, no joint friction, (reorient_backends plant spec kp4_kv0_fr1_fl0_dp0.08). A gain measurement needs a known torque on a joint (Section 7).

Relative contact-velocity control of the three-finger turn

The question was whether the hand-object controls of Wang, Oh and Pollard can carry out our reorientation, in which all three fingers move the tool together, in place of the deployed open-loop joint trajectories. The scene is the bench maneuver of each deployed hand D1–D8: palm fixed, the 25 mm, 24.5 g tool lying on its post, the plan’s grip held 0.8 s, the working plant, the TPU tip as 1 mm pads in MuJoCo and as a compliant convex ( = 10 MPa, relaxation 0.01 s) in Drake. Placements: seed 0 at the plan’s pose, seeds 1–4 jittered by 2 mm and 2° (MuJoCo 5 placements per hand, Drake 3).

Controller

At 100 Hz the controller reads the nine joint angles and the tool pose, poses a kinematic MuJoCo copy of the scene with the TPU block as one convex mesh per tip, and builds the paper’s contact frame per finger : origin at the closest points of block and tool (mj_geomDistance), the tool’s surface normal toward the finger, the finger’s flexion axis projected on the tangent plane. The paper commands relative contact velocities (finger minus tool at the contact). For a turn that keeps all three contacts, each contact’s reference is the velocity of the tool’s material point under the desired tool motion, so the relative velocity is zero while the tool follows, plus a normal term that regulates the pad force:

(1)

Here is the tool turn, the horizontal axis normal to the starting tool axis, the tool axis and the starting axis turned by about , the tool’s material point at the starting centroid of the three contacts and that point 5 mm above its start, and the contact point and normal of finger , its pad force from the simulator’s contact solution and  N; , . The paper’s Eq. 2 then gives each finger’s joint rates by bounded least squares:

(2)

with  mm, , , , and the translational and rotational Jacobians of finger at its contact point, the grip pose, and bounds from the joint limits and  rad/s. Algorithm 1 is one control tick. The reference turns at 30°/s toward vertical after a 0.5 s squeeze in which the plan’s 5–13 N grip relaxes to 2 N, and the rollout ends 2 s after the reference stops. Code: scripts/hom_turn3.py; the same controller drives MuJoCo and Drake.

On the working plant the deployed open-loop plans hold the tool on 40 of 40 MuJoCo placements and turn it 27–57° (hand medians); Drake holds 24 of 24 and turns within a few degrees of MuJoCo. The drops and the near-zero turns in the films of the previous page came from that page’s plant (, 1 s fingers, ).

Newton’s hydroelastic contact on the same fingertip shape, with its stiffness divided by the tip–tool effective mass (Section 4), holds the tool on 33 of 40 placements (column F).

With its governor the HOM controller holds 40 of 40 placements in MuJoCo and 24 of 24 in Drake, but stops at 6–42° (hand medians), short of the plan on every hand. Without the governor the reference runs on to vertical: the tool reaches held peaks of 27–60° and is dropped by the end on 6 hands (D1, D2, D3, D4, D6, D8). The governor stopped 31 of 40 MuJoCo rollouts on a pad losing force and 9 with a pip joint at a limit. In the rollouts without it, the pip joints sat at a rate or position bound in a median 85 % of control ticks (the most-saturated pip of each rollout). The deployed grips start the pips at 0–3° on seven hands (D1: 19° and 41°) against an extension limit of −18°, so keeping three contacts fixed on a turning tool asks the fingers for extension they lack, and the least-loaded pad lets go first. With fixed contacts on these grasps the controller does not reach vertical; it needs a grasp chosen for the turn (pips flexed at the start) or a change of contact mode partway, such as one finger sliding along the tool or a regrasp.

Placement sensitivity: the governed turn depends on how the grip settles before the reference starts. An earlier squeeze phase that ramped the force target up from 0 N let D7 reach 52–65° on all five placements and dropped D1 on two of five; the rows above use the version that holds 2 N from the start.

Grasp search by turn range

The turn range of a grasp is the largest rotation of the tool toward vertical, about the horizontal axis normal to its starting axis through the contacts’ centroid (the rotation the controller commands), at which, for every smaller angle in 3° steps, each fingertip still reaches its tool-fixed contact point (inverse kinematics of the finger’s three joints puts its pad point within 1 mm of the contact, inside the joint limits less a margin, with the pad normal within 45° of the tool’s surface normal) and pad forces exist that hold the tool (a linear program over the three contact forces: they balance the tool’s weight and moments, lie in the friction pyramid with at least 0.5 N normal, and load no finger joint beyond the 1 N m servo limit). The grasp is the tool’s offset on its post (±12 mm along its axis, ±5 mm across, ±15° yaw) and each finger’s contact on the cylinder (position along the axis and angle around it); CEM with 96 samples, 8 elites and 15 iterations maximises the range from the deployed grip’s contacts (scripts/hom_grasp_search.py, rows grasp_search.jsonl, turn3_best_grasp.jsonl). The controller then starts from the searched grasp: grip targets from the inverse kinematics at 0° with each pad commanded 2 mm into the tool, fingers starting with the pads 8 mm outside their contacts (from the plan’s open pose, the 3°-margin grasps knocked the tool off its post).

The search raises the range from 3–18° to 18–81° (8° margin). The searched grasps move the index and middle contacts toward the tool’s centre (9–32 mm from it against 35–46 mm) and start those pips at −10 to 62°. The controller does not carry them out: from the 8°-margin grasps the tool is held in 3 of 18 rollouts (13 lose it during the grip) and the held ones turn it −10 to −8°, away from vertical; from the 3°-margin grasps 7 of 18 hold. Most rollouts lose the tool during the grip, which the kinematic score leaves out.

Effective-mass scaling of Newton’s hydroelastic stiffness

Newton passes each hydroelastic contact point to MuJoCo-Warp with a force stiffness in N/m (the point’s share of the pressure field: patch area times the two shapes’ in series). SolverMuJoCo writes it as a solref time constant, damping ratio 1 and solimp (newton/_src/solvers/mujoco/kernels.py, lines 599–618 at Newton commit 009158e). MuJoCo treats solref as a spring on the constraint acceleration, so the contact holds per metre of penetration, not :

(3)

Newton’s shape-material path multiplies its stiffness by the inverse-weight sum before the same conversion (docs/solvers/mujoco.rst, “Shape-material contact stiffness and damping”); the hydroelastic path does not, and the ShapeConfig.kh docstring (newton/_src/sim/builder.py) says that SolverMuJoCo scales the stiffness by masses and that should be tuned with that in mind. The MuJoCo sphere pads already divide out: each pad reaches its stiffness at relaxation through the solimp impedance

(4)

which uses the same inverse weights (reorient_backends.replace_tips); this is why they matched Drake without fitting. The correction is therefore , with the inverse weights read from the solver’s own MuJoCo model (solver.mj_model.body_invweight0 through solver.mjc_body_to_newton); stays a material constant.

On the 2026-10-05 contact bed (two 20 g pads on rails pinching the 24.5 g tool, rows docs/experiments/20261006-newton_mass_scaling/, contact_bed_newton.py models newton_hydro_mc*) the solver’s model gives each pad an inverse weight of 16.7 1/kg and the tool 40.7, so = 17.4 g and uncorrected Newton sank 7.1–7.4 times as deep as Drake with 2.4–2.6 times Drake’s onset torque. Multiplied by 57.4 1/kg, Newton sinks 1.02–1.04 times Drake’s depth and reaches 0.76–0.88 of its onset torque, with no parameter fitted. Inverse weights from a separate MuJoCo compile of the bed’s MJCF give a factor of 90.7 and over-stiffen the contact (sink 0.82–0.83 times Drake), so the factor has to come from the solver’s model.

The deployed turn with the correction

In the turn scene each fingertip (4.9 g, the same body in Newton’s model and the MJCF) has an inverse weight of 2.18 1/kg, the finger chain and its servo armature seen at the tip, and the tool 40.7; = 23.3 g, so each tip’s is multiplied by 42.9 1/kg and the tool’s is 100 times the largest tip (scripts/newton_turn.py --mass-correct). The deployed plans then hold the tool on 33 of 40 placements (35 in a run of the same placements on 2026-10-06), against 10 of 40 uncorrected (Table 3, column F; uncorrected rows plans_newton.jsonl, 9 of the 40 lost the tool during the grip). 25 of the held placements turn the tool more than 10°. On 8 (D3 seeds 1, 3, 4; D5 seeds 1, 2, 3; D8 seeds 1, 3) the tool stays in the grip but turns less than 5°. 2 placements (D1 seed 1, D6 seed 1) drop the tool during the 0.8 s grip and 5 lose it during the turn. Where the tool turns, the hand median is within 5° of MuJoCo on D1, D2, D3, D4, D6; 8–33° short on D5, D7, D8.

Agreement of five contact models with Drake

Figure 5 compares five fingertip contact models with Drake’s hydroelastic contact (the TPU block as a compliant convex, = 10 MPa, Section 3) on three tasks with one fingertip shape (the TPU block with 2.7 mm fillets), one control method (open-loop replay) and one sphere packing (0.75 mm spheres at 1 mm): the twist and the brake on the two-pad contact bed of 2026-10-05, and the plan replay of the three-finger turn on D1–D8, paired with Drake by hand and placement (placements 0–2, 24 pairs). The models are the 1 mm pads in CPU MuJoCo, in MuJoCo-Warp (reorient_backends_gpu.py; bed model mjw_pads1 in contact_bed_newton.py) and in Newton’s point-contact pipeline (newton_turn.py --contact pads; bed model newton_pads1), Newton’s hydroelastic contact on the plain block with divided by the effective mass (Section 4), and MuJoCo point contact on the block mesh (condim 3). Rows: docs/experiments/20261006-simulator_agreement/; figure scripts/simulator_agreement_figure.py.

Newton needs two settings carried over for the pads to be the same model as MuJoCo’s. The pads’ solimp (Eq. 4) holds the inverse weights of the model it was computed on; Newton’s import gives the bed’s railed pads 16.7 1/kg against the MJCF compile’s 50, so is recomputed from the solver’s model (0.866 → 0.788); on the hand the two sets of inverse weights agree to . For elliptic cones SolverMuJoCo also sets every contact’s friction-row time constant from the shapes’ friction gain (kernels.py, “force-space friction slope”):

(5)

with the impratio, where MuJoCo gives the friction rows the pads’ own solref,  ms. Newton’s importer sets , which gives  s; with it the braked tool swung to 108°, past hanging. With set so that (4.4 on the bed, 5.8 on the three fingertips) the swing matches MuJoCo’s.

The three pad implementations agree with Drake to the same degree: onset torque 0.94 of Drake’s, largest swing within 1.1° of Drake’s, and grip force 0.98–1.53 of Drake’s. CPU MuJoCo and MuJoCo-Warp turn the tool within 3° of Drake on 23 and 23 of 24 pairs and hold every placement; Newton’s pads turn within 3° on 22 of 24 pairs and hold 40 of 40 placements. The mass-corrected hydroelastic contact reaches 0.76–0.88 of Drake’s onset torque, swings the braked tool to 130°, turns within 3° on 7 of 24 pairs and holds 33 of 40 placements. Point contact holds every placement of the turn, but its onset torque is 0.05–0.16 of Drake’s and the braked tool spins out of the pinch; its turns fall within 3° of Drake on 11 of 24 pairs.

Cost of sphere-pad fingertips in RL training

The RL comparison asked for here trains the reorientation with the pad fingertip and with the point contact every run so far has used, then replays the policies in Drake and Newton. Before training, the cost. The environment is the D6 reorientation env of the RL pipeline (mjlab on MuJoCo-Warp 3.6: scripted grasp and lift, 2 ms step, 10 physics steps per policy step, elliptic cone, impratio 10, 10 solver and 20 line-search iterations) on morphology runs that differ only in the fingertip (make_pad_morphology_run.py). The pads touch only the tool; the block’s convex mesh takes the floor and finger-to-finger contacts (with pads colliding with everything, a 2 mm pad tip resting on the floor made up to 738 contacts per world). Tip and distal-link inertias are pinned to the source run’s, so the mass distribution is unchanged. Contact buffers are sized from a calibration pass and grown when MuJoCo-Warp reports an overflow. Zero-action env steps, timed after 60 warm-up steps that cover the grasp.

Table 7. Throughput of the D6 RL training env per fingertip model (scripts/rl_contact_throughput.py, rows docs/experiments/20261006-rl_contact/throughput.jsonl). Contacts/world: largest count in one world after the grasp. GPU memory: nvidia-smi with the env alive. ‘Incomplete’: the run ran out of GPU memory in a process holding earlier envs and was stopped by the memory watchdog when repeated alone.

Physics is a small part of an env step: at 2,048 envs the box tip’s physics takes 10 % of the wall time, the rest is observation, reward, sensor and termination code. The 1 mm pads make physics 1.9× slower per world-step at 1,024 envs and the env 11 % slower at 1,024 envs and 12 % at 2,048; the 2 mm pads cost 2 % at 2,048. GPU memory grows with the pads: 6.2 GB for the 1 mm pads at 2,048 envs and 10.5 GB for the front-half pads at 4,096, against 4.4 GB for the box tip at 4,096; the full 1 mm pads at 4,096 envs did not complete. Throughput does not grow past 2,048 envs for any fingertip.

Contact sensor for sphere pads

The fingertip and palm contact sensors now sum every matched contact (mjlab reduce="netforce", a world-frame vector) and the simulation allocates 256 matches per sensor (contact_sensor_maxmatch; mjlab’s default of 64 overflowed with the pads), set in src/morphohand/rl/env_build.py. Before, each fingertip reported one contact chosen by match order (reduce="none", one slot): the whole force of the box tip, one pad’s share on the pad tip. Every consumer (grip-force, force-excess, force-spread and brace rewards, contact gates, tip-lost terminations, the deploy read-outs) takes the vector norm and found > 0, so the change of frame does not reach them. Regression (scripts/rl_contact_sensor_check.py, rows docs/experiments/20261006-rl_contact/sensor_check.jsonl): on the box tip the old and new sensors, read side by side in one env for 200 steps at 64 envs, give every sensor-reading reward term the same value (largest difference 0) and force norms within 1.9e-06 N; no fingertip had more than one matched contact. On the 1 mm pads (8 envs, 4 instants after the grasp, 96 fingertip samples, up to 31 pad contacts per tip) the sensor equals the sum of the pad contact forces of the same GPU solve to 2e-07 and a CPU MuJoCo re-solve of the same state to 0.2 %. At 2,048 envs the env runs 9,295 (box tip) and 7,912 (pads) env steps/s with the summed sensor, against 9,439 and 8,329 in Table 7 with the one-contact sensor.

The env has no mass randomisation. Adding one requires recomputing each pad’s solimp per world, since holds the inverse weights of the nominal tip and tool. The compliance randomisation (randomize_geom_solimp) overwrites and is off in the configuration the training below copies.

Physics cost on one held RL state

Each engine starts from the same state of the RL env: D6 after its scripted grasp and lift (60 zero-action policy steps, 64 worlds, every tool held; with 1 mm pads 41 contacts and 132 constraint rows per world), exported with mjlab’s scene writer (scripts/rl_state_export.py; free-body positions relative to each world’s grid origin, which mjlab adds per world). Every engine loads that MJCF with each body’s compiled inertia pinned, the trainer’s options (2 ms, implicitfast, elliptic cone, impratio 10, 10 solver and 20 line-search iterations), the exported joint angles tiled over the batch, the exported servo targets and zero velocity, and steps 22 graph-captured blocks of 50 steps (scripts/same_state_timing.py, rows docs/experiments/20261006-rl_contact/same_state_timing.jsonl). Newton 1.7.0.dev0 uses its own collision pipeline (contact gap 0.5 mm, margin 0), the TPU block re-added as a mesh from its OBJ, and for hydroelastic contact on the tips multiplied by the tip–tool of its solver model (Section 4; tip inverse weights 4.95–5.14, tool 39.1 1/kg), 100 times that on the tool, 0.5 mm grid, ±6 mm band, contact reduction, buffers at 1.3 % of Newton’s defaults. The pads’ solimp in Newton is recomputed from its solver model’s inverse weights, which equal the MJCF compile’s to , so is unchanged. The first rows run the live mjlab env for the same number of steps; its step includes the contact sensors.

Table 8. Physics wall time per world-step on one held state of the D6 RL env, by number of worlds. Contacts and constraint rows per world at the end of the 1,024-world run; lowest holding: the smaller fraction of worlds whose tool stayed within 20 mm of its exported position over the 2.2 s run. Shaded: fewer than 95 % held. Not run: MuJoCo-Warp 3.14 pads at 2,048 worlds (GPU memory) and Newton pads at 2,048 (its model build takes 7.5 GB of host memory at 1,024).

The 1 mm pads cost 2.41 µs per world-step in MuJoCo-Warp 3.6 from this state (mjlab’s env 2.98) and hold every tool. The 17–26 µs and 13 % drops measured earlier on the bench grip came from two settings of the raw MuJoCo-Warp script: rerun with both corrected, the bench grip costs 3.19 µs with 122 contacts per world and holds 100 % (rows newton_throughput.jsonl). First, it forced the SAP_SEGMENTED broadphase; MuJoCo-Warp’s put_model, and therefore mjlab, chooses NXN over the contype-filtered geom pairs when they number under 250,000, and the pads touch only the tool, so the pair list is short. On this state SAP costs 16.7 µs. Second, the broadphase writes its candidate pairs into the per-world contact buffer, and on the pads they exceed 250 per world for about 43 contacts; a buffer of 123 contacts per world overflowed and dropped pad contacts, and 52 % of worlds lost the tool. With 512 contacts per world both versions hold every tool; MuJoCo-Warp 3.14 takes 1.75 µs.

Newton’s mass-corrected hydroelastic tip holds every tool at 4.25 µs per world-step (1,024 worlds; 4.34 at 2,048, 8,351 MB of GPU) with 41 reduced contact points and 131 constraint rows per world: 1.8 times the MuJoCo-Warp pads at 1,024 worlds and 4.5–6.8 times point contact on the box tip at 2,048. Newton with sphere pads takes 4.00 µs; its 0.5 mm contact gap reports 259 pad contacts per world, of which about as many become constraint rows as in MuJoCo-Warp. Newton’s point contact on the block mesh loses the tool in 51 % of worlds at 2,048, as it did at 4,096 on the bench grip.

RL training: TPU block mesh against 1 mm pads

The D6 reorientation trained from scratch with the b_liveA recipe and the flags of the 2026-09-17 60 M run (results/rl/20260917-1141-d6_cal_reorient_gp025_60M_s0/config.yaml; a dry-run diff leaves only the number of envs, the step budget and the checkpoint interval), on scenes with the working plant (scripts/make_work_plant_runs.py: finger kp 4 N m/rad, kv 0, 1 N m, damping 0.08, frictionloss 0, ) and two fingertips: the TPU block as one convex mesh (point contact) and as 1 mm sphere pads (65 / 39 / 18 pad contacts on thumb / index / middle in the zero-action grasp). Both scenes lift and hold the tool in 64 of 64 envs with zero residual actions. Two seeds per fingertip (the trainer’s --seed is now applied: it seeds python, numpy, torch and Warp through the env config; the GPU contact solve stays non-deterministic), 20 M steps at 2,048 envs, friction randomised 0.55–1.15× per env, checkpoints every 41 iterations (2.0 M steps), one run at a time (scripts/rl_contact_train_queue.sh). Every checkpoint is rolled out deterministically in 64 envs for 250 policy steps without randomisation (scripts/rl_contact_eval.py over policy_eval_suite.py, rows docs/experiments/20261006-rl_contact/train_eval.jsonl).

With the TPU block mesh (point contact) the final policies end at cos 0.636–0.688 (47–51° from vertical), holding the tool in 60 and 64 of 64 rollouts; 0 of 128 reach cos 0.9. The cosine still rises over the last 4 M steps on 2 of 2 runs. 2 runs lost the tool in every rollout at an intermediate checkpoint before recovering. With the TPU 1 mm pads the final policies end at cos 0.431–0.438 (64° from vertical), holding the tool in 64 and 64 of 64 rollouts; 0 of 128 reach cos 0.9. The cosine still rises over the last 4 M steps on 1 of 2 runs. 2 runs lost the tool in every rollout at an intermediate checkpoint before recovering.

The films (Figures 7–10) show one rollout of each final policy. With the mesh tip both seeds raise the middle finger’s end of the tool once the residual acts and reach their angle by step 90: 39–43° above horizontal (from the mean final cosine). The middle fingertip rides on the raised end, the thumb pushes under the middle of the shaft and the index holds the low end; the tool stays at that angle to the end of the episode. Seed 0 drops the tool in 4 of 64 rollouts at a mean step of 231, and 4 pass cos 0.9 at a mean step of 229: the tool swings upright as the grip opens, then falls; the first render of this checkpoint caught one such drop. With the 1 mm pads both seeds roll the thumb along the shaft and hold the tool at 26°; seed 1 brings the thumb back under the shaft after step 170 without turning it further. The pads load the thumb and index more and the middle finger less (mean contact force from step 58: thumb 26–28, index 21, middle 6–8 N, against 21, 11–12 and 9–10 N with the mesh tip). The pad policies turn the tool 16° less on average and hold it in every rollout of both seeds, with a final-cosine spread (sd over 64 rollouts) of 0.009 and 0.029, against 0.227 and 0.008 with the mesh tip.

The final policy’s finger targets from the reorientation onset (step 58) of world 0, replayed open loop for 3.84 s on a bench-like copy of the RL scene (palm fixed at its lifted pose; scripts/rl_policy_replay.py, rows policy_replay.jsonl): final cosine of the tool with vertical when it is still held, else the time the tool fell below 60 mm. CPU MuJoCo reproduces the pad policies within 0.02 in cosine of MuJoCo-Warp and holds the tool. From the same onset state it ejects the tool of both mesh-tip policies within 0.3 s, also when the onset servo targets are held constant, although the three block contacts penetrate only 0.2–0.3 mm there; the point contact of a convex block on the cylinder does not carry over between the two MuJoCo implementations. Drake and Newton, both with the plain block, follow the mesh policies through the turn (Newton at 1 ms: cos 0.5–0.64 for the first 1.4 s) and lose the tool before the end in three of four replays; Drake holds one at cos 0.588. The pad policies replayed on the plain block in Drake and Newton turn the tool toward the other pole (Newton: cos −0.59 and −0.83, held) or drop it.

Next measurements

  1. Servo gain with a known load. At the bench, with the servo holding a commanded angle, hang 50, 100 and 200 g from a fingertip on a measured lever and read the deficit from the servo readback; the slope is in N m/rad. The replays cannot give it (Table 2). A 20° free-air step per joint at 111 Hz gives ; anything above 0.2 s falsifies the working plant.
  2. Grasp search scored after the grip. In hom_grasp_search.py, simulate each CEM candidate’s 0.8 s grip in MuJoCo (1 mm pads, working plant) and score the kinematic turn range from the pad contacts the grip actually reaches, rejecting candidates whose tool leaves its post or whose pads end more than 2 mm from the planned contacts. A searched grasp that the governed controller turns past the deployed grasp’s angle on D7, D2 and D5 (6, 42 and 23°) would confirm grasp choice as the limit; none would point at the controller.
  3. A second contact mode in the HOM controller. When a finger’s pip reaches its limit, give that finger’s contact a slide reference along the tool axis while the other two hold; measure the reachable turn and the drop rate on the same 40 placements.
  4. Newton’s turn without rotation. Log the per-finger normal force and the tip slip speed in newton_turn.py and compare them with MuJoCo’s pad forces on D3 (seeds 1, 3, 4), D5 (seeds 1, 2) and D8 (seeds 1, 3), where the mass-corrected Newton grip holds the tool but turns it less than 5°.
  5. Friction rows of Newton’s hydroelastic contact. The 2026-10-05 friction gain gives the hydroelastic friction rows a time constant of 3.9 ms on the bed (Section 5). Run contact_bed_newton.py brake --models newton_hydro_mc with set for = 2, 5, 10 and 20 ms (Eq. 5); the pads’ 108° swing became MuJoCo’s 88° at 10 ms. A setting at which the hydroelastic swing falls within 3° of Drake’s 87.3°, rerun on the turn’s 40 placements, would show whether the 130° swing and the two drops during the grip come from the friction rows.
  6. Longer training. Both fingertips are still rising at 20 M steps (Figure 6). Continue the four runs to 60 M (the 2026-09-17 budget) from their final checkpoints with the critic and optimizer warm-started, and compare the held cosine at 40 and 60 M; a pad run that stays below the mesh runs by more than their seed spread (0.05) at 60 M would make the fingertip model, not the budget, the difference.
  7. Mesh-tip contact between MuJoCo-Warp and CPU MuJoCo. At the replay onset state of the mesh runs, list the three block–tool contacts (position, normal, depth, efc force) in both implementations (rl_policy_replay.py record’s scene and same_state_timing.py’s GPU arrays); a normal that differs by more than 10° between them would explain the CPU ejection.
  8. Newton under the learned grip. Log the per-tip hydroelastic force and the tool slip in the Newton replay of the mesh policies and compare with the MuJoCo-Warp recording; the drop after 1.2–2.8 s on a grip of 20 N on the thumb is the next Newton discrepancy.
